passage:
Chetan, your parents told me you've been asking questions about the puja, and that they're frightened. Sit. I'm Saurabh, and I was twenty once.

I stopped joining the evening aarti and one day said, "Why waste an hour on this?" My mother's face fell. My father went silent. Later I heard her tell a neighbour, "We've lost him."

That hurt. That night I sat with her and said, "Amma, I love you. I'm not leaving anything. I just have questions." I still ate the prasad she handed me. A week later I asked my father, gently, what the aarti gave him.

He said, "It's how my mother sat with me." We never agreed on everything. But after that, nobody in the house was afraid.

qa.q: What did Saurabh's mother say to a neighbour?
What were Saurabh's parents feeling when he stopped joining the aarti?
qa.a: They were afraid: his mother's face fell and she told a neighbour they had lost him, while his father went silent.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do that eased the fear, and what else could Chetan try?
qa.a: Saurabh told his mother he loved her and only had questions, ate the prasad, and asked his father gently what the aarti gave him; Chetan could share questions the same gentle way. 🙂

qa.q: What might the aarti mean to Saurabh's father?
qa.a: It seems to be a memory and a closeness, since he said it is how his mother sat with him, not a challenge to Saurabh.

grounding: Saurabh's parents fear his questions mean he is losing his way, and he reassures them, shares gently and avoids mocking their rituals.

passage:
Zeenat: Ammi cried tonight
Disha: what happened??
Zeenat: I said I'm not sure I believe everything anymore. just that. and she asked if college had changed me into someone else
Zeenat: Abbu didn't say anything. just went to pray
Disha: that must've hurt
Zeenat: I never wanted to hurt anyone. I love Ammi and Abbu so much
Disha: have you told them that part?
Zeenat: no. I just argued about the questions
Disha: maybe start with the love bit. tell them you're still you. same values, same Zeenat
Disha: and share the questions slowly, not all at once
Zeenat: my roommate said I should tell them it's all superstition
Disha: please don't. that would feel like mocking them
Zeenat: yeah. ok. tomorrow I'll make chai for Ammi before fajr like I used to and just sit with her 🤍
Disha: that sounds right

qa.q: What did Ammi ask after Zeenat spoke?
qa.a: Ammi asked if college had changed Zeenat into someone else.

qa.q: What is Zeenat feeling after Ammi cries?
qa.a: Zeenat feels hurt and guilty, not wanting to hurt parents Zeenat loves so much.

qa.q: What did Disha suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Start by saying Zeenat still loves them and is the same person, share questions slowly, and never mock their beliefs, so their fear can ease.

qa.q: How do Zeenat's parents seem to see the questions?
qa.a: They seem afraid that college has changed Zeenat and pulled Zeenat away from the family's way.

grounding: A chat shows parents frightened by a child's questions about faith, and a friend advising reassurance of love, gentle sharing and no mockery of their beliefs.

passage: In their small town near Bankura, Bidisha's father, Shankar, heard from a neighbour that she hadn't kept the Shivratri fast at her college hostel. That evening he sat on the verandah without eating. 'Is this what the city teaches? Next you'll stop touching your grandmother's feet.' Bidisha felt her face burn. A sharp answer was ready: that fasting was just habit. She had said something like it to a friend once and hated how it sounded. Instead she sat on the step below him. 'Baba, I have questions. I'm reading, I'm thinking. But I haven't stopped loving you or Thakuma, and I haven't stopped being honest or kind. Those came from you.' He looked at the tulsi plant, not at her. 'And the puja?' 'I'll help Ma prepare it on Sunday, like always. I may not believe everything the way you do. I'll still be there.' After a long while, he picked up his plate.

qa.q: How did Shankar find out about the fast?
What was Bidisha feeling when her father spoke?
qa.a: Bidisha felt her face burn with hurt and embarrassment, and was tempted to answer sharply.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say that eased her father's fear?
qa.a: That she still loved him and Thakuma, still held the values they taught, and would help with Sunday's puja, sharing her questions gently.
Shankar fears the city is pulling Bidisha away from the family's ways and values.

grounding: Shows a father afraid that his daughter's questions mean losing her values, and her reassuring him of her love while sharing doubts without contempt for the rituals.
